stories.title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
stories.titleZh: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later
stories.author: zulln
summaryZh: Thousands of flights were canceled or delayed Saturday morning as airlines struggled to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. departures for more than four hours Friday.By 9:30 a.m. ET Saturday, flight tracking service FlightAware had logged more than 3,700 cancellations and 1,990 delays. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Chicago O’Hare International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport were among the hubs experiencing the most disruptions, according to FlightAware.The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and airports across the country filled with stranded passengers. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines said Friday evening that they were resuming flights.A senior government official told NBC News on Saturday that the system that caused the outage had been identified and taken offline. The FAA said a router sent too much data, overloading older air traffic control equipment.What caused the ground stopTransportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday evening that controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and communications with aircraft at 3:36 p.m. ET. The FAA issued the ground stop at 3:54 p.m. ET, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”Duffy said the FAA retained some radar and communications capabilities and halted departures as a precaution. Medical flights, including those transporting organs for transplant, were allowed to continue.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday night that authorities had found no evidence of a cyberattack.“FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said in a news conference from the White House Friday night. Earlier on Friday, he described the issue as a telecommunications outage.Why disruptions continued SaturdayAirlines had to get planes and crews back into position after the ground stop, and some crews may have reached limits on how long they could stay on duty. Duffy said he expected air traffic to recover before the Thanksgiving rush.But by 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport had run out of room to park aircraft and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, a source with knowledge told NBC News.Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”Werne said he began hearing from friends who were also stuck on planes, including one on a runway in Chicago. His plane headed back to the terminal so passengers could get off.02:31Friday’s ground stop is perhaps the most severe consequence of what Duffy described as a decades-old air traffic control system that uses analog equipment, which has led to several issues and outages over the past few years.In May 2025, radar screens at Newark Liberty International Airport went black during a 90-second outage.Duffy said the legacy equipment will continue to fail and pushed Congress to approve $50 billion to overhaul the system. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion over five years to upgrade air traffic control, Reuters reported.Mullin said although authorities cannot rule out a cyberattack, there was no evidence to suggest there was one. “There’s nothing completely certain right now. It doesn’t appear that way,” he said.Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.Duffy said the SMART system is “completely disconnected” from the equipment that suffered issues Friday.Several hours after the ground stop was announced, a top aviation expert estimated that anywhere from 300,000 to 400,000 passengers were stranded — and it was anybody’s guess when they would get to their destinations.Chicago O'Hare International Airport, filled with waiting passengers.Jacek Boczarski / Anadolu via Getty“Daily, we have about 25,000 flights in U.S. domestic markets,” Vikrant Vaze, a Dartmouth professor who specializes in commercial aviation logistics, wrote in an email to NBC News. “I would say we should have around 3,000 to 4,000 flights held up at this time over the past 2 plus hours.”With planes stranded on runways, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary.”Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are the ones affected by the outage.02:41Nationwide ground stops are extremely rareGround stops across the nation are a rarity in U.S. history.After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights for a few hours, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.Officials at the time blamed contract personnel for the outage, saying they accidentally deleted files while working to correct the synchronization between databases. The error prompted a computer outage that lasted approximately an hour and a half, Department of Transportation officials said at the time.

comments.textZhHtml:
Ex-MSFT here, sharing my outdated POV based on working on a product that was using Microsoft Exchange and therefore was hooked onto the email delivery pipeline.

Note that the infra for M365, Azure etc is different. They would be running on servers hosted in MSFT DCs but have completely different CI/CD pipelines. M365 services have their own deployment pipelines and it takes on the order of weeks to deploy your changes to production.

Considering the fact that Outlook is down, clearly email doesn’t seem to be working. So email uses something called Microsoft Exchange Server, there used to be an on-premises version of this but MS stopped supporting it to run the cloud version hereby called M365. Email is one big “macro-service”, if you’re running Windows Server, look at the process called “EdgeTransport.exe” this is responsible for sending/receiving email on Windows Servers. There are probably multiple 100s of services supported by 100s of teams that are run while email is routed from sender to receiver via MSFT Exchange servers. My recollection is that even if one of these services goes down or introduces latency in the pipeline, it caused a major incident. When I was working in M365 Security in 2024, this Exchange Server pipeline was called “legacy” because it’s one big .NET Framework service. I don’t know if they upgraded to .NET core but developing on this was as HN comments say, very janky.

The reason Teams doesn’t seem to be down is that Teams services are completely different and are written using .NET Core and have their own separate release pipeline. It was much easier to interact with Teams services. I actually worked closely with the team that was responsible for ingesting Teams messages to the customer’s data store. Their code base was much more modern and easy to understand. Exchange Server not so much.

I don’t know if what I said is accurate but know that Exchange server code was like a fossil that didn’t change as much, over the ~5 years I worked on it from 2019-2024.

Story time over.

stories.titleZh: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
stories.author: speckx
summaryZh: Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC.

The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions. The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.

comments.author: Silfen
comments.textZhHtml:
Reading this thread makes me realize that seemingly no one has heard the basic, mundane case for why Nvidia would want to do so much "circular financing" as a matter of totally normal business strategy. This may not be the whole story, but it's worth understanding.

Because of bottlenecks in the supply chain, Nvidia knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory. They could raise prices quite a bit more, but then their only customers would be hyperscalers (building competing chips) and possibly OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia is willing to forgo present day profits for the strategic value of keeping its customer base diverse and promoting the network effects of e.g. CUDA. Instead of quoting a lower price per GPU to neoclouds and startups, they finance purchases of chips, but the two are roughly equivalent (financing means Nvidia takes on more risk, but has more upside and locks in future demand). It is in their commercial interest to have many competing buyers of their chips.

Obviously this creates fun mechanisms for fraud and wacky accounting (and I'm agnostic as to whether that's happening here), but it's worth knowing about the boring/obvious story before donning your tinfoil hat.

It of course, wants to keep all customers happy… but some will get much more soup than others.

This is probably a huge factor in keeping their advantage over their customers and competitors (but I repeat myself.) That is, TPUs and Trainium etc simply cannot acquire the necessary volume of chips at a competitive enough price-point to put a dent in Nvidia’s grip on the market. But the hyperscalers need all that compute NOW NOW NOW, so they have no choice but to turn around and begrudgingly pay Nvidia for that supply. Which puts more cash flow in Nvidia’s pocket, which buys them more soup, and on this loop continues.

stories.titleZh: Nvidia employees petition to bring back Jensen Huang
stories.author: lavendermon
summaryZh: Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.Got a Tip?Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24.Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

stories.author: ayhanfuat
summaryZh: November 11, 2026, 5:36am 1 I am immensely sad to announce that Tim Peters has died earlier this year on July 15. It’s hard to overestimate Tim’s influence on Python. He’s probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that. Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing. Tim quickly became a major phenomenon on the Python mailing list (including later incarnations and spinoffs), where he earned the nickname “Timbot” by his innumerable, careful and patient answers to user questions. These he filled with mild humor (always marked by <wink> or <0.5 wink>) and often referred to as “channeling Guido”. At the same time Tim participated in numerous in-depth design discussions, saving me or others from embarrassing design mistakes or solving deep problems, guided by his vast mathematical knowledge and compiler-building experience. In fact, Tim really set the tone for early core development, never outright dismissing people and explaining in detail why things could or couldn’t work. In 2002, Tim gave us Timsort: a new sorting algorithm he designed for Python lists, which was later adopted by Java and Android. Python-would-not-be-what-it-is-today-without-Tim-ly y’rs, –Guido

comments.author: glimshe
comments.textZhHtml:
I remember that back in the 80s, when I was still deciding what I wanted to do when I grew up, there was a distinction between a "programmer" and a "systems analyst".

The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

The programmer, supposedly a lower paid profession, transformed that into Computer code. I remember someone telling me that wasn't the best choice and that I should become a "systems analyst". They wore the better suits.

My college even offered a shorter, cheaper degree for people who just wanted to be "programmers".

I think this distinction still survives in government labor statistics.

Perhaps we came full circle with LLMs partially killing the "programmer" job.

comments.author: xorcist
comments.textZhHtml:
We might be the same generation, I recognize the two roles. What I also remember is just empirically how much better the "programmers" were at doing the "system analysts" job. Way, way better. Then we stopped educating system analysts and now the job title is not heard of anymore.

I regularly meet (recently examined) people who are trained "software architects". Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project. The best programmers are just so much better software architects also. So I expect history to repeat at this point.

comments.author: EarthBlues
comments.textZhHtml:
Programmers are better architects because their decisions are continually informed by experience from the "sharp end" of the system.  LLMs don't really have experiences, I dont think its the same.
Our profession will likely shake out a lot of people in the coming years.  What will be left may not be a classic "systems analyst" or "architect" role. I think the people who stay in this field will have to move both up and down the abstraction stack simultaneously -- our job will become a lot more "real", physical, relational, risk-oriented.  I dont think there's good reason to believe LLMs can supply the need for prudence in the fields where software is deployed.

comments.author: saltcured
comments.textZhHtml:
In my opinion, a lot of that "no longer getting it" is because of the social/fashion trends that continually disrupt programming.

You don't forget CS concepts so easily, but all the syntactic tricks of new language variants and working set vocabulary of APIs, data formats, and frameworks keeps churning away from whatever you last had contacted in a real, hands-on way.

It is fascinating, wondering where this is going as programmers turn into their own middle managers on top of agents. Particularly, the school who claim that you don't really need to understand all the code and instead treat it like a black-box experiment. If this fad takes over the main stage, then everyone becomes one of those less technical managers.

But, in this new scenario, there is no human in the loop to inject judgement calls and "manage up" anymore. There is no programmer culture except the models and agents, which don't really have the same social connections to drive a programming culture. What will happen? A culture per agent product? Per enterprise client of the agent vendor? Per agent operator? Per codebase?

> Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project.

Negative value to the project, perhaps; but if these "software architects" are kept around despite several rounds of this, it may be because they're providing positive value to the company, in terms of producing for the company a thing whose existence (no matter how flawed) serves as collateral for:

- the executive team, to show to investors, to convince them that they're acting strategically in the market; or

- the marketing team, to get breathless puff-piece articles written about the company, in places where dumb CTOs/CIOs who make IT buying decisions will read them. (Not necessarily to then buy the specific product that came out of that project — hopefully not, in fact! — but instead to remember the company itself the next time they're comparing vendors for something else);

- or the executive team again, this time to show to a potential acquirer, to convince the acquirer that their employees have a higher asset value for having a certain skill / experience with certain paradigms, that they gained working on this project.

Companies have spent collective billions (trillions?) of dollars on projects they know will go nowhere, just to be able to say they did a project that is made a certain way or does a certain thing or has certain certifications, and to have a shitty codebase they can pull out of their back pocket if needed to back that up. In all such cases, even if they need to present the product, the product will never be evaluated for its quality or for its fit-for-purpose-ness; so it doesn't matter that the project failed to produce something of quality or that is fit-for-purpose. It just matters that the project happened.

I think both definitions are still too narrow for what I do daily. I fully agree that we still need humans to decide what to build, how it should all fit together, etc.

But both definitions do not really take into account the huge social dimension of being a good (computer) engineer in a company. You have to translate requests from a wild variety of users into what this means for a system. You have to recognize and explain that what they need is not always what they think they need. You have to be able to say "no" to things. All these things are very hard for an LLM (reading humans, not literally following requests).

Then there are social aspects like building consensus within a project, building a user base of many people that are initially skeptical, using existing relations with people and other companies to slowly adopt what you are building, etc.

Programming used to be a large chunk of the work. I thoroughly enjoyed this aspect of the work when I was younger, but at some point I started enjoying system design and everything around it more. So in that sense, programming with LLMs is much nicer (though I still review every single line of code and often have to go through a couple of iterations because even Opus 5.5 often doesn't get it 'right' in the first take). But the remaining part of the work is extremely hard for an LLM to replace.

comments.author: retwakm4
comments.textZhHtml:
I prefer to call myself a programmer because I don't think we (as a class) consistently perform a lot of the types of duties (both ethical ones and just basic job performance ones) that would be required of a lot of engineering disciplines.

I also started out in systems programming and we still call ourselves programmers there, when there is a lot of systems "engineering" (aka trying not to blow up the system with your code running in supervisor state) going on. And there, a lot more attention paid to stuff like IEEE code of ethics, professional development, rigorous designs, etc.

So I'll keep to calling myself programmer amongst my non software engineering friends. It just seems more humble.

That being said, writing the code has like others have pointed out, never been the largest part of the job in my experience. So I can see how it may be confusing to some, especially software engineers. But to non software engineers I think they mostly get it...you are a software engineer trying not to imply some some sort of unearned intellectual superiority.

comments.author: fweimer
comments.textZhHtml:
Well, OpenOffice wouldn't print on Tuesdays:

“ What a fascinating bug!! My wife has complained that open office will never print on Tuesdays!?! Then she demonstrated it. Sure enough, won't print on Tuesday. Other applications print. I think this is the same bug. Here is my guess:

Print to a postscript file. Observe the line: %%CreationDate: (Tue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Change "Tue" to anything else: %%CreationDate: (XTue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Save the file and it prints. Tools like evince work because they simply omit the "CreationDate" tag to begin with.

Now something odd happens when my cups script (I am using the Brother MFC420CN) copies the file to a temp file. Some of the code is rearranged, not sure how or why, but it uses a command called "file" to identify the file as "PostScript". This check would work on the original file you printed, but by the time it runs the check on the temp file, it misidentifies. Normally it would return:

   PostScript document text conforming at level 3.0
But there is another check that happens before the PostScript check. If it finds "Tue" at the fourth byte of the file, it identifies it as:

   Jan 22 14:32:44 MET 1991\011Erlang JAM file - version 4.2
So it's not a problem w/ openoffice.org, cups, or the brother printer drivers. It is a bug in the `file` utility, and documented at https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/file/+bug/248619. ”

https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/cupsys/+bug/255161...

I'm having trouble understanding your question in the context of the discussion, so I will talk about the topic generally instead.

Imagine a server allows you to upload images. It has a system designed for images only. It will behave unpredictably maybe even dangerously with another file. The server checks that the file ends with .jpg. it checks that the file is a valid jpeg. All clear. Upload allowed. But 5 steps later some tool looks at the image file and notices it's a valid zip file (creating files with multiple valid interpretations is something people have succeeded in doing it's not always so hard). It runs this check before the image check. The next step in the processing chain wants an image but it has been told it's dealing with a zip file. So it unzips the file to see if it contains an image. But it was a zip bomb. The server goes down.

stories.title: Rust 1.100
stories.author: mbStavola
summaryZh: The Rust team is happy to announce a new version of Rust, 1.100.0. Rust is a programming language empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, you can get 1.100.0 with: $ rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website, and check out the detailed release notes for 1.100.0. If you'd like to help us out by testing future releases, you might consider updating locally to use the beta channel (rustup default beta) or the nightly channel (rustup default nightly). Please report any bugs you might come across!

comments.author: nirinor
comments.textZhHtml:
Woohoo, that's a release! My personal favorites:

- Stabilize never type

- Stabilize custom allocators

- Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335

- cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388

comments.author: SOLAR_FIELDS
comments.textZhHtml:
Dependency cooldowns receiving such a whiplash this year. Earlier everyone was advocating for them because of the supply chain attacks. Now, people are worried because you might miss 0 days if you use them.

Nonetheless, the ability to set and configure it is a welcome feature.

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.textZhHtml:
You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down, and you should immediately patch security advisories.

One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

comments.author: kragen
comments.textZhHtml:
Usually people advocate dependency cooldowns as a mitigation for supply-chain attacks, where you're depending on a module with a malicious maintainer, possibly a new one (perhaps one who stole the old maintainer's keys so they can pretend to be the old maintainer).

In that situation, how do you distinguish between "normal updates" (that you should let cool down) and "security advisories"? If all the hypothetical malicious maintainer has to do to get you to update is to publish a security advisory for their own package, wouldn't they just do that? It might even be a real advisory about a real security hole that they introduced, but claiming more versions are affected than actually are affected.

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.textZhHtml: It takes additional permissions, in general, to issue an advisory. And “supply chain” attacks in general tend to be used by smash-and-grab attackers, who don’t have time on their side. It’s not like a browser 0day where the attacker’s goal is to preserve their underlying exploit primitive for as long as possible.

comments.author: kragen
comments.textZhHtml: Additional permissions?

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.textZhHtml: I’m talking about things like GHSAs. You can’t issue one just by compromising a push credential to a repository, which is how most of these supply chain attacks start.

comments.author: jmvoodoo
comments.textZhHtml:
Waiting for someone to hold back a vulnerability until they can compromise a package, then release vuln publicly for maximum impact.

It’s only a matter of time.

comments.author: ninkendo
comments.textZhHtml:
How do you separate security advisories from regular updates? (If it’s just a box you check, it only means attackers will say “this is a security update” on the malicious package they upload.)

The point of cooldowns is for when a crate author’s account is compromised and used to publish malicious code. Saying “security advisories bypass cooldowns” wouldn’t really help anything there.

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.textZhHtml:
> If it’s just a box you check, it only means attackers will say “this is a security update” on the malicious package they upload.

It generally requires additional permissions, per the adjacent respond. And it introduces additional scrutiny on the release, which is the last thing an opportunistic attacker wants (the entire reason “supply chain” attacks are effective is because nobody gives any thought to upgrading their dependencies in the normal case).

comments.author: PaoloBarbolini
comments.textZhHtml: There are many cases in which security advisories aren't published. But I guess an alternative could be to update using the cooldown, and then diff the dependencies that would get a newer version if the cooldown wasn't in place to check if they contain anything relevant for the particular application you're developing.

comments.author: derefr
comments.textZhHtml:
Why wouldn't a supply-chain attacker simply manipulate the project into producing a security advisory to get their exploit code pushed through inside a high-priority release?

I.e. get a puppet/co-conspirator to push vulnerable code; wait until that code gets released as v1.2.3; submit other vulnerable code; wait for that code to be merged and released as v1.2.4; then submit a vuln report for the vuln introduced in v1.2.3; and wait for v1.2.3 + v1.2.4 to be security-deprecated and v1.2.5 to be fast-released to replace them.

Now v1.2.5 exists and has your still-unknown 0day in it, while versions prior to v1.2.5 are deprecated. If devtools that had pinned v1.2.3 get forced "upward" to v1.2.5 despite the cooldown, you win.

comments.author: dns_snek
comments.textZhHtml:
I haven't seen anyone advocate against cooldowns because those are completely different problems.

How would removing cooldowns help you patch vulnerabilities? That would imply that your CI is configured to update dependencies, rebuild, and push them to production without human oversight?

That's obviously not the way to go, you must have human oversight and if you do then your humans should be alerted when one of your dependencies patches a security issue. At that point you review it, override the cooldown, and push it to production.

comments.author: zarzavat
comments.textZhHtml: You should use a cooldown. The effects of a supply chain attack are significantly worse than the effects of a 0 day. You can always make exceptions on a case-by-case basis.

comments.author: saghm
comments.textZhHtml: Some of us were saying they didn't understand the endgame of everyone using cooldowns at the time. We mostly got told we were wrong though.
